Chapter 1—Growing Up in a World That Doesn’t See You.
It often starts with a feeling you can’t quite put your finger on.
Picture this: a child, full of wonder, stepping into a classroom for the very first time. The walls? They’re plastered with maps and posters—celebrating far-off places and faces that don’t look anything like theirs. The teacher’s stories, the books on the shelves, even the games in the playground... everything seems to point away from the world that child knows best.
There’s this quiet message, whispered over and over in little moments: if you want to belong, if you want to be accepted, you’ve got to become someone else.
And honestly, that’s the start of a journey nobody ever asks for—yet so many are pushed into. The world, shaped by the legacy of colonial history, has already made up its mind about what’s normal, what’s beautiful, and what’s worthy.
If your skin isn’t white, or your language isn’t the one that holds power, the message comes through loud and clear: you’re different, and that difference? Well, it’s seen as a problem that needs fixing.
As that child gets older, the feeling just grows. And it’s not just about being left out of a game or a story. It’s about hearing—again and again—that everything about you... your hair, your accent, your family’s traditions... is somehow not enough.
So, you start to watch, to listen, to try and fit in. Deep down, there’s this longing: to be noticed, to be valued, to be part of a world that seems to run on rules you never even helped write.
Now, at home, things are different. There’s laughter, warmth, a true sense of belonging. But even there, the outside world finds a way in. Parents worry about how their kids will be treated. They urge them to speak “properly,” to dress a certain way, to keep a low profile.
The child picks up on this tension—a mix of pride in who they are, and fear of what the world might do to them.
As time goes on, the child grows up. The questions just get bigger, and the risks feel higher. In job interviews, out on the street, or even in relationships, those old patterns keep showing up. Sometimes it’s a look, or a word, or a door that never quite opens. Other times, it’s more subtle—just that nagging sense that no matter what you do, you’ll never really measure up.
Most folks don’t see any of this. If you fit the mold, the world can feel totally natural—even welcoming. But if you’re on the outside, every day is a negotiation. Do you speak up or stay silent? Try to blend in, or stand out? Do you hold tight to your roots, or loosen your grip in hopes of finally being accepted?
This... this is what it’s like to live in a world built on colonial ideas. It’s not just about laws or politics. It’s about the stories we hear, the images we see, and the ways we end up seeing ourselves. These wounds? They run deep, and they don’t just disappear.
But here’s the thing—even when it hurts, there’s a stubborn kind of hope that refuses to die. The belief that things can change. That dignity is possible. That being seen for who you truly are... is always worth fighting for.
